 Georgia makes changes to SNAP EBT cards following social media influencer’s indictment 
 DHS blocks online and out-of-area purchases by default and mails new cards inactive. Its written answers did not describe changes to identity checks, mailing addresses or bank accounts. 
 By Anastassia Olmos Published : Nov. 15, 2026 at 9:57 PM EST | Updated : 1 hour ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) - An electronic benefits transfer (EBT) phone line cited in a federal food stamp fraud case is back online with new monitoring systems, according to the Georgia Department of Human Services (DHS). DHS also has added two EBT card security features following the federal indictment of social media influencer, Mercedes New. 
 Federal prosecutors said New, known online as “Shawty Dred,” contacted the state’s EBT phone line more than 9,000 times to fraudulently obtain more than $4 million in SNAP benefits. 
 New is accused of using stolen identities to obtain more than 500 EBT cards. DHS mailed the cards to at least four different addresses around Metro Atlanta, loading a total of $4.6 million in taxpayer dollars into the accounts from 2020 to 2026, according to the indictment. 
 DHS said it cannot comment on open investigations or prosecutions, but confirmed changes to the phoneline system and two new card-lock safety measures. It did not state any changes to identity verification or monitoring EBT recipients linked to one bank account.
 Read the full investigation HERE 
 What DHS says it changed 
 A week after New’s arrest, DHS said it implemented two EBT card features on Oct. 22, 2026: 
 Online purchases and purchases outside Georgia and its five bordering states are blocked by default. Cardholders who need those purchases must unlock their cards. 
 New and replacement EBT cards are mailed inactive. 
 Cardholders can lock and unlock their cards through the ConnectEBT website or app, or by calling the EBT call center at 1-888-421-3281, according to DHS. 
 Atlanta News First Investigates asked DHS whether it had made security changes to prevent the type of fraud New is accused of committing. 
 “DHS prioritizes security enhancements for the program, and the EBT IVR call center is now back online with new monitoring systems requested by DHS with the goal of improved security,” a DHS spokesperson said. 
 DHS also cited a $748,573 U.S. Department of Agriculture grant awarded in September 2025, the second-highest SNAP Fraud Framework Implementation Grant that year. The agency said it is using the money for a multiyear project that includes public outreach and “specialized fraud prevention tools and training for agency staff.” 
 EBT phone line security
 Georgia DHS allows participants to access their cards through an automated phone line. EBT recipients can use the internet and telephone to report lost cards, request replacements, check balances and change PINs. 
 Atlanta News First Investigates asked DHS when it first identified the alleged attack, what weaknesses it found and what safeguards flag a single phone number, device or address linked to unusually high numbers of accounts or transactions. DHS’s written responses did not answer those questions. 
 “He was a one-man fraud ring,” said Haywood Talcove, who leads the government business at LexisNexis Risk Solutions, a company providing fraud detection and identity tools to government agencies, including in Georgia. “The technology the state is using is antiquated… He was making those phone calls to check the balance of the cards before he cashed them out. That should have raised a level of suspicion.” 
 Talcove said EBT recipients should register a phone number and that a call from any other number should not be allowed to get a balance. 
 “That’s a pretty simple fix,” he said. 
 What a fraud expert says about the changes 
 LexisNexis Risk Solutions sells fraud and identity tools to government agencies, and Talcove has said the company works with Georgia. 
 “Georgia deserves credit for taking steps to improve EBT card security,” Talcove said in a statement to Atlanta News First Investigates. “Blocking certain transactions, issuing inactive replacement cards, and increasing monitoring of the telephone system are positive developments.” 
 He said that, based on the allegations in the federal case, “this wasn’t simply someone stealing an EBT card or guessing a PIN.” Prosecutors allege about $4.6 million in benefits was diverted through fraudulently established accounts, with multiple cards and replacement cards sent to addresses associated with the scheme. 
 Talcove said the case raises these questions: 
 How were so many accounts established without detecting the connections between them? 
 Why weren’t repeated requests, common addresses and unusual account activity flagged? 
 What identity verification was performed before benefits were issued or account information was changed? 
 What controls existed to prevent someone from repeatedly exploiting the telephone system? 
 On the phone line, he said: “Georgia says it has added monitoring to its IVR system. That’s encouraging, but monitoring alone isn’t enough. The real question is whether the system can identify suspicious behavior and stop fraudulent transactions before taxpayer dollars leave the program.” 
 Talcove said agencies should: 
 Verify identity, residency, household eligibility and other application information with independent, authoritative sources instead of relying on self-reported information. 
 Identify connections between applications, addresses, accounts, devices and transactions that may indicate organized fraud. 
 Require additional identity verification for high-risk changes. 
 Investigate unusual patterns before more benefits are issued. 
 Use independent third-party audits to continuously test whether controls work. 
 Strengthen controls over SNAP retailers, including ongoing monitoring and verification of compliance. 
 “I don’t want to minimize the improvements Georgia has made,” Talcove said. “But based on what the state has publicly described, I haven’t seen evidence that it has addressed the underlying weaknesses allegedly exploited in this case.” 
 “Taxpayers deserve more than assurances that security has improved,” he said. “They deserve measurable results showing that criminals can no longer exploit the same vulnerabilities.” 
 In an earlier interview with Atlanta News First Investigates, Talcove said EBT recipients should register a phone number, and that a call from any other number should not be allowed to get a balance. He also said states should require chip cards. 
 DHS said changes to the EBT system, including chip-enabled cards, require approval by and coordination with federal partners, along with adherence to state law and procurement processes. DHS said other states are rolling out chip cards and that it is working with federal partners and other states to learn from them. It did not give a rollout date.
 What the indictment describes and what DHS said 
 Indictment or Justice Department DHS written response 
 False applications listed names, dates of birth and Social Security numbers of people who did not authorize their use. Did not describe changes to identity verification. 
 Cards and replacement cards were mailed to metro Atlanta addresses, including the store address. When New requested replacements, he “provided or otherwise confirmed the mailing address,” the indictment says. New and replacement cards are now mailed inactive. Did not describe changes to how mailing addresses are verified or changed. 
 Phone numbers associated with New contacted the automated line more than 9,000 times and reached more than 350 accounts, according to the Justice Department. Line is “back online with new monitoring systems.” Did not say what the monitoring does. 
 About $660,000 in SNAP benefits was transferred to Shawty Dred LLC’s bank account, the indictment says. Did not mention bank accounts. 
 East Point police seized 14 EBT cards from New at a Walmart on Nov. 29, 2025, and charged him under state law, according to a police report and jail records. Among its examples, the indictment lists replacement cards mailed to the store address on Dec. 3, Dec. 11 and Dec. 18, 2025, and March 5, 2026. It also lists a card issued in New’s name and mailed to the same address March 24, 2026. 
 Who pays when benefits are stolen 
 SNAP benefits are federally funded and that each state certifies household eligibility and issues the benefits. 
 DHS said federal authority to replace stolen benefits ended Dec. 20, 2024. It said benefits stolen on or after Dec. 21, 2024, are not eligible for replacement. 
 “The state has no further recourse with the end of this federal program,” DHS said adding that it funds nonprofit feeding partners across Georgia. SNAP customers can find resources at feedinggeorgia.org/our-food-banks , according to DHS.
